'''Roger Thomas Staubach''' ({{IPAc-en|s|t|ɔː|b|ɑː|k}}, -{{IPAc-en|b|æ|k}}; {{respell|STAW|bahk|}}, -{{respell|back}}; born February 5, 1942), nicknamed "'''Roger the Dodger'''", "'''Captain America'''", and "'''Captain Comeback'''",<ref>{{cite web |last=Weintraub |first=Robert |title=OTL: Game in the Shadows |url=http://www.espn.com/espn/eticket/story?page=texas1964 |access-date=March 13, 2024 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 11 seasons with the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He attended the [[United States Naval Academy|U.S. Naval Academy]], where he played [[college football]] for the [[Navy Midshipmen football|Navy Midshipmen]] and won the 1963 [[Heisman Trophy]]. After graduation, he served in the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], including a [[Vietnam War|tour of duty in Vietnam]].

Staubach joined the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in [[1969 Dallas Cowboys season|1969]], becoming the team's second major [[Franchise player|franchise]] quarterback after the retirement of [[Don Meredith]] in 1968. Staubach played with the Cowboys during his entire career. He led the team to the [[Super Bowl]] five times, four as the starting quarterback. He led the Cowboys to victories in [[Super Bowl VI]] and [[Super Bowl XII]]. Staubach was named [[Super Bowl Most Valuable Player|Most Valuable Player]] of [[Super Bowl VI]], becoming the first of four players to win both the Heisman Trophy and [[Super Bowl MVP]], along with [[Jim Plunkett]], [[Marcus Allen]], and [[Desmond Howard]]. He was named to the [[Pro Bowl]] six times during his 11-year NFL career. Staubach is one of ten players to both win the Heisman Trophy and be elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame, and the only quarterback.<ref name="profootballhof.com">{{cite web |title=Heisman Hall of Famers |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2017/12/news-heisman-hall-of-famers/ |access-date=March 21, 2023}}</ref>

Upon his retirement Staubach founded The Staubach Group, a commercial real estate firm that he later sold to [[Jones Lang LaSalle]] for $613 million in 2008. He then became executive chairman of the Americas region of Jones Lang LaSalle until his retirement in 2018. That same year, he received a [[Presidential Medal of Freedom]].

'''Roger Russell Wehrli''' ({{respell|WUR|lee}}; born November 26, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire 14-year career as a [[cornerback]] for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1969 until 1982. He was a seven-time [[Pro Bowl]]er after playing [[college football]] for the [[Missouri Tigers football|Missouri Tigers]], where he was a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] and a first-round draft choice by the Cardinals in 1969. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2003 and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2007.

'''Roger Lewis Finnie''' (November 6, 1945 – August 6, 2012) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] and [[defensive tackle]] who played eleven seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Finnie played [[college football]] for [[Florida A&M University]].<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/players/rogerfinnie/profile?id=FIN652597 Roger Finnie]</ref>

Finnie was an All-City team member at [[Miami Northwestern Senior High School]] and a key factor in Northwestern's state championship in 1964. At [[Florida A&M University|Florida A&M]], Finnie garnered All-Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference and [[All-America|All-American]] honors.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=October 6, 1990 |title=1990 FAMU Sports Hall of Fame Inductee Profiles |url=http://famu.digital.flvc.org/islandora/object/famu%3A80 |journal=Strike |pages=33}}</ref>

Finnie was selected by the [[New York Jets]] in the 14th round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]]. He began his [[National Football League|NFL]] career as a [[defensive tackle]] and also played offensive [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] and [[tight end]] with the Jets. He was traded to the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] in [[1973 NFL season|1973]] where he was converted to a full-time [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]]. Finnie played left tackle on a record-breaking offensive line that included [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] member [[Dan Dierdorf]], [[Conrad Dobler]], [[Tom Banks (American football)|Tom Banks]], and [[Bob Young (offensive lineman)|Bob Young]]. That unit led the NFL with the fewest [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] allowed for three years (and the [[National Football Conference]] for five years) in the mid-1970s. In [[1975 NFL season|1975]], the group set an NFL record, allowing only eight sacks in 14 games. The Cardinals traded Finnie to the [[New Orleans Saints]] in [[1979 NFL season|1979]] where he was reunited with former teammate Dobler.<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 3, 1979|title=Big Red's Finnie traded To Saints |pages=4C and 6C |work=St. Louis Post Dispatch |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/139518325 |access-date=August 3, 2022}}</ref> He retired in 1980.

After retirement, Finnie resided in Miami and served as a Coordinator for the Summer Youth Employment and Training Program, also working as a Senior and Youth Counselor. He also coordinated the city football league for boys ages 15 and under and was commissioner of the Miami city basketball team. He was inducted into the [[Florida A&M University|FAMU]] Hall of Fame in 1990.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=October 6, 1990 |title=1990 FAMU Sports Hall of Fame Inductee Profiles |url=http://famu.digital.flvc.org/islandora/object/famu%3A80 |journal=Strike |pages=33}}</ref>

Finnie died in 2012 at the age of 66.

'''Roland Harper''' (born February 28, 1953) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] for eight seasons with the [[Chicago Bears]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisiana Tech Bulldogs football|Louisiana Tech Bulldogs]] before being selected in the 17th and final round of the [[1975 NFL draft]].  He was a starting [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] known in his playing days as a punishing blocker who opened holes in opposing defenses for star halfback [[Walter Payton]].  Harper ranks sixth on the Bears' all-time rushing list with 3,044 yards and 15 TDs on 757 carries in seven seasons.<ref name=pfr>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HarpRo00.htm|title=Roland Harper|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |accessdate=2008-12-28}}</ref><ref name=fraud/> Harper was inducted into the [[Louisiana Tech University Athletic Hall of Fame]] in 1986.

Although he was selected in the final round of the 1975 draft, Harper wound up as the Bears starting fullback that season.<ref name=bears>{{cite web|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=838|title=Catching up with ... Roland Harper|date=January 19, 2005|accessdate=2008-12-29|archive-date=2009-01-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090119070936/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=838|url-status=dead}}</ref>  He was joined in the backfield that season by fellow rookie Payton, who was the Bears first round draft choice that season.<ref name=Payton>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PaytWa00.htm|title=Walter Payton|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref>  Fellow rookie [[Bob Avellini]], the Bears sixth round draft pick in 1975, also started several games at [[quarterback]] that season, giving the Bears an all rookie backfield.<ref name=Avellini>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/A/AvelBo00.htm|title=Bob Avellini|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref>  Harper, Payton and Avelleni started most of the games for the Bears together from 1976 through 1978.  In his rookie season, Harper rushed for 453 yards on 100 carries.<ref name=pfr/>  His 4.5 yards per rushing attempt ranked 7th in the [[NFL]] that season.<ref name=pfr/>  He also caught 27 passes for 191 yards in 1975.<ref name=pfr/>

In 1976, Harper started all 14 games and increased his rushing yards total to 625 on 147 carries, for a 4.3 yards per carry average.  He also caught 29 passes for 291 yards.  In 1977, Harper rushed for 457 yards on 120 carries, a 3.8 yards per carry average, and caught 19 passes for 142 yards.<ref name=pfr/>

Harper's best season was 1978, when he rushed for 992 yards on 240 carries, for a 4.1 yards per carry average.<ref name=pfr/>  Since Payton rushed for 1,395 yards that season, he fell just eight rushing yards short of making the [[1978 Chicago Bears season|1978 Bears]] the 3rd NFL team and 1st NFC team to have [[List of NFL teams with multiple 1000-yard rushers|two players with at least 1,000 rushing yards]] (after the [[1972 Miami Dolphins season|1972 Miami Dolphins]] and the [[1976 Pittsburgh Steelers season|1976 Pittsburgh Steelers]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1978.htm|title=1978 Chicago Bears|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |accessdate=2008-12-28}}</ref>  He also caught a career-high 43 passes that season for 340 yards, and set another career high by scoring eight [[touchdown]]s (six rushing, two receiving).<ref name=pfr/>  His 1332 total yards from scrimmage ranked 10th in the NFL that season, and his 240 rushing attempts also ranked 10th in the NFL.<ref name=pfr/>

Harper missed the entire 1979 season due to a knee injury.<ref name=Neft79>{{cite book|title=The Sports Encyclopedia: Pro Football|author=Neft, D., Cohen, R. & Korch, R.|year=1995|page=354|publisher=St. Martin's Press |isbn=0-312-13186-0}}</ref>  However, he returned in 1980 and started 12 games.  In 1980, he rushed for 404 yards on 113 carries for a 3.6 yards per carry average and caught just 7 passes for 31 yards, but his blocking helped Payton run for 1,460 yards.<ref name=pfr/>  Although Harper played in 15 games in 1981, he was supplanted as the starting fullback for most of the season by [[Matt Suhey]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/chi/1981.htm|title=1981 Chicago Bears|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref>  He rushed for just 106 yards on 34 carries (a 3.1 average) and caught just two passes all year for ten yards.<ref name=pfr/>  Harper's final season was 1982, when he played in eight games, rushed for seven yards on three carries, and caught one pass for eight yards.<ref name=pfr/>

After his playing career ended, Harper continued to live in the Chicago area.<ref name=bears/>  Since 1990, he ran Rohar Trucking and Excavating, a company that does snow removal, trucking, transporting construction materials and erecting steel.<ref name=bears/>  The company helped build the [[Luxury box|skyboxes]] at [[Soldier Field]], the Bears' home field.<ref name=bears/>

In June 2008, Harper pleaded guilty to one count of [[mail fraud]].<ref name=fraud>{{cite web|url=http://www.iht.com/articles/ap/2008/06/18/sports/FBN-Bears-Harper-Plea.php|title=Former Bears FB Harper pleads guilty in landscape scam|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|date=June 18, 2008|accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref><ref name=usnews>{{cite web|url=https://www.usnews.com/blogs/the-collar/2008/6/19/ex-chicago-bears-fullback-admits-fraud.html|title=Ex-Chicago Bears Fullback Admits Fraud|publisher=[[U.S. News & World Report]]|author=Mullins, L.|date=June 19, 2008|accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref><ref name=upi>{{cite web|url=http://www.upi.com/Sports_News/2008/06/18/Ex-Chicago_Bears_back_Harper_pleads_guilty/UPI-24341213806695/|title=Ex-Chicago Bears back Harper pleads guilty|publisher=[[United Press International|UPI]]|accessdate=2008-12-29}}</ref>  The fraud allowed Monahan Landscape Co.. a white-owned firm, to receive a $1.5 million Chicago Public Schools landscaping contract that was supposed to be reserved for minority-owned firms.<ref name=fraud/>  The plea also revealed that Rohar was controlled by Monahan.<ref name=fraud/>  In June 2009 he was sentenced to two years [[probation]], including one year [[house arrest]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Roland Harper Trusted Too Much |publisher=[[NBC]] Chicago|url=http://www.nbcchicago.com/news/sports/Roland-Harper-Trusted-Too-Much.html|author=Hendricks, M.|date= June 10, 2009|accessdate=2010-03-04}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|publisher=[[WBBM (AM)|WBBM 780]]|url=http://www.wbbm780.com/Ex-Bear-Roland-Harper-to-be-sentenced-for-fraud/4562930|title=Ex-Bear Avoids Prison|date=June 9, 2009|accessdate=2010-03-04}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref>

'''Rodney Tate''' (born February 14, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]]. He played in the NFL for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] from 1982 to 1983 and for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in 1984. <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TateRo01.htm |title=Rodney Tate Stats |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com |date= |access-date=2019-12-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/player/rodneytate/2527042/profile |title=Rodney Tate, RB |work=Nfl.com |date= |access-date=2019-12-30}}</ref>

Tate was a top recruit out of Beggs High School in 1978 and part of the 1975 State Championship Team and also won multiple state championships in track for sprinting. Though recruited by home-state Oklahoma he made the unusual choice of going to the [[University of Texas]].<ref name="Beggs">{{cite news |last1=Kemp |first1=Adam |title=Former Beggs star Rodney Tate is one of the few Oklahoma high schoolers to head south of Red River |url=https://www.oklahoman.com/story/sports/high-school/2018/10/04/former-beggs-star-rodney-tate-is-one-of-the-few-oklahoma-high-schoolers-to-head-south-of-red-river/60497439007/ |access-date=8 February 2023 |date=4 October 2018}}</ref>

At [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas]] he played both football and ran track. During his senior year, the Longhorns spent one week ranked #1 and finished the year ranked #2 after beating Alabama in the Cotton Bowl. Though frequent injuries kept him off the field, getting only 170 touches over 4 seasons, his explosive speed caught the attention of NFL Scouts.<ref name="tate">{{cite web |title=Rodney Tate |url=https://wearebeggs.com/rodney-tate/ |access-date=8 February 2023}}</ref>

In track he set the school record, later broken, in the 60 yard dash.<ref>{{cite web |title=Texas Track and Field Record Book |url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/texassports_com/documents/2019/2/18/2018_19_TFXC_Record_Book_Final.pdf |access-date=8 February 2023}}</ref>

In the NFL, he returned a kick-off return for 101 yards during a preseason game, but saw little playing time in his two years in Cincinnati and less in Atlanta.

After the NFL he returned to Texas to get degrees in sociology and communications and work as a graduate assistant coach hoping to catch on in college football coaching, but no offers came. He returned to his home town to run a lawn care business with his brother and then became a football, track and cross-country coach at his old high school, helping them to get to the 2017 state championship game.<ref name="Beggs"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Helsley |first1=Jeff |title=A Texas-sized steal Tate chose Longhorns over OU - with no regrets |url=https://www.oklahoman.com/story/news/2000/01/16/a-texas-sized-steal-tate-chose-longhorns-over-ou-with-no-regrets/62213927007/ |access-date=8 February 2023 |date=16 January 2000}}</ref> In 2022, the school named their football stadium for him.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Horton |first1=Stacey |title=FOOTBALL FIELD NAMED FOR FORMER NFL PLAYER |url=https://www.beggs.k12.ok.us/article/844736 |access-date=8 February 2023 |date=22 September 2022}}</ref>
